title: The river that changed its mind
teaches: Why bends grow and cut off, braided and meandering rivers, log jams and avulsion
summary: **Water corkscrews round a bend.** Fast surface water is driven toward the outside bank and plunges down it, and slower water near the bed returns toward the inside: the secondary flow Thomson described in 1876 and Einstein matched to a teacup in 1926.
**The outside of a bend erodes and the inside builds.** The plunge digs a pool and a steep cut bank; the flow along the bed carries sand and gravel to the inside, where it settles as a point bar.
**A bend, once started, grows.** A sharper bend drives a stronger secondary flow, which eats the outside bank faster, so loops swell and travel down the valley.
**Loops end in cutoffs.** When a loop doubles back until only a neck of land is left, a flood cuts across it and the old loop is left as an oxbow lake.
**Banks set the pace.** Roots slow a bend's growth, bare banks let it run, and riprap stops it; how a straight river starts to bend in the first place is still argued.
**Steep rivers with heavy loads braid.** Where the slope is steep and the gravel supply large, as on the White, Carbon and Hoh, a river splits into many threads around shifting bars.
**Gentler rivers with banks held by mud and roots meander.** For the same flow, a meandering river runs on a gentler slope than a braided one, and it carries less coarse sediment.
**Log jams steer rivers.** A jam scours pools, splits the flow and, during a flood, can tip a river out of its channel.

**An avulsion is a river jumping to a new course.** A river that has built its bed up above the land beside it can be sent down to lower ground by a jam or a flood, as the White River was at Auburn in 1906.

blocks.text: Until the autumn of 1906, the White River, grey with silt from the glaciers of Mount Rainier, came out of the foothills at Auburn, took in the Green and turned north. Together they wound down the Kent valley past the farms, took in the Black River from Lake Washington, and reached Elliott Bay in Seattle as the Duwamish. A few kilometres to the south, across a valley floor so flat that a farmer could hardly tell which way it sloped, a smaller channel called the Stuck ran the other way, south to the Puyallup River and on to Tacoma.

In November 1906 a flood came down every river around the Sound. Driftwood piled up where the White spread out onto the valley floor near Auburn and jammed across its channel. When the water went down, the White was running south down the Stuck into the Puyallup. It had gone to bed flowing to Seattle and woken up flowing to Tacoma.

blocks.caption: Where the White River went: before the flood of November 1906, after it, and once the diversion at Auburn held it. Rivers drawn by hand over the relief, so their courses are approximate.

stages.label: Before 1906
stages.text: The White leaves the foothills at Auburn and turns north with the Green, down the Kent valley to the Duwamish and Elliott Bay. The Stuck (dashed) is a small channel running south to the Puyallup.

stages.label: November 1906
stages.text: Driftwood jams the channel near Auburn during the flood. The water spills south down the Stuck, and when the flood is over the White is flowing to the Puyallup and Tacoma instead of to Seattle.

stages.label: About 1915
stages.text: The two counties have agreed to keep the river where the jam sent it, and a concrete diversion at Auburn holds the White in the Stuck channel. Only the Green runs north to the Duwamish now.

blocks.text: King County's farmers were pleased, since the river that had flooded the Kent valley every winter was gone. Pierce County, downstream on the Puyallup, was not, and the two counties argued over it for years. In the end they agreed to keep the river where the jam had sent it, and by about 1915 a concrete diversion at Auburn held the White in its new course, where it still runs. The Duwamish had lost most of its water, which the Seattle branch (S3) follows.

A pile of logs cannot push a river uphill. Before reading on, think about what the jam must have done, and what the valley floor must have been like for it to work. The answer needs a few ideas about how rivers choose their paths, starting with a cup of tea.

Stir a cup of loose-leaf tea, take the spoon out and watch the leaves on the bottom. You might expect the spinning water to fling them outward, the way a spin dryer throws clothes against its drum. They slide inward instead, and gather in a little heap in the middle.

blocks.caption: A stirred teacup from above (left) and cut in half (right) in the seconds after the spoon comes out. Choose how hard to stir, then watch. A model: the swirl dies away in about ten seconds, and the slow loop across the cup grows with the square of the swirl's speed.
blocks.task: Stir hard, then play the seconds after the spoon comes out

blocks.text: Albert Einstein explained this in a short paper in 1926, written to answer a question about rivers.[^baer] Spinning water presses outward, so it piles a little higher at the rim than in the middle: the surface of a stirred cup is a shallow dish. The extra height at the rim pushes back inward with the same force at every depth. Near the top, the water swirls fast and its outward push wins, so it moves out. At the bottom, the water rubs on the cup and slows, its outward push weakens, and the inward push from the dish wins. So the bottom water creeps inward, carrying the leaves, rises up the middle and turns outward again at the top. This slow loop across the cup rides on top of the spin. The leaves are too heavy to ride up the middle with it, so they are left in a heap.

James Thomson, an engineer and the elder brother of Lord Kelvin, had described the same loop in river bends fifty years earlier, in 1876.[^thomson] Water going round a bend is water going round a cup. The surface stands a little higher against the outside bank, fast water near the surface is driven toward the outside bank and down it, and slower water near the bed returns toward the inside. Seen from above, the water corkscrews round the bend. A loop like this, across the channel and riding on the main downstream flow, is called **secondary flow**.

blocks.caption: A river bend seen from above, and cut across at its sharpest point, looking downstream. Fast surface water runs toward the outside bank and down it; the flow along the bed returns toward the inside. Depths are exaggerated about ten times.

blocks.text: The water plunging down the outside bank does the digging. It scours a deep **pool** at the foot of the bank and undercuts it until slabs of earth and trees fall in, leaving a steep, raw **cut bank**. The flow along the bed sweeps sand and gravel toward the inside of the bend, the way the cup's bottom flow sweeps leaves to the middle, and drops them where the water is shallow and slow. Flood by flood, the inside of the bend grows a gently sloping beach of sand and gravel, a **point bar**.

blocks.title: On a riverbank
points: Find a bend on the Snoqualmie at Fall City or at Tolt-MacDonald Park in Carnation, or on any river with bends, in late summer when the water is low.
On the outside of the bend, look for a steep bank with roots hanging out of it and trees leaning over the water. That is the cut bank, and the water at its foot is the deepest in the reach.
On the inside, look for the low beach of gravel and sand sloping gently into shallow water. That is the point bar, where people fish and picnic, and its stones get finer toward the top of the bar.

blocks.text: Erosion on the outside and building on the inside make a feedback. The channel moves sideways toward the outside of its bend; as it moves, the bend gets sharper; a sharper bend drives a stronger secondary flow; and the stronger flow eats the outside bank faster. A bend, once started, grows.

Bends do not simply swell in place. The fastest water hits the outside bank a little downstream of the sharpest point of the bend, so the erosion is shifted downstream too, and bends creep down the valley as they grow. Each year's point bar leaves a low curved ridge of sand on the inside of the bend. Seen from the air, an old floodplain is combed with these ridges, called **scroll bars**, a record of where the channel used to run.

blocks.caption: A river meandering across its floodplain, seen from above, over a few centuries. The pale lines are where the channel ran every 25 years. Choose what holds the banks, then play. A model: each stretch of bank moves at a rate set by the bend of the river just upstream of it, with the bank's strength as a brake.
blocks.task: Guess, then play until the river cuts off a loop

blocks.text: Sooner or later a growing loop doubles back on itself until only a narrow neck of land separates one bend from the next. A flood pours across the neck and the river takes the short cut, a **neck cutoff**. The old loop, plugged with sand at both ends, becomes a curved lake, an **oxbow lake**, which slowly fills with mud and plants. The floodplain of the Snoqualmie between Fall City and Duvall is scattered with old loops and sloughs of this kind, easiest to see on a lidar map of the valley.[^lidar]

How fast this happens depends on the banks. The roots of alders, willows and cottonwoods bind a bank together, so a forested bank erodes far more slowly than a bare one. Rock dumped along a bank, **riprap**, stops it altogether, which is why it lines the outside of bends wherever a road or a house stands close to a river. A river that cannot move sideways puts its energy into its bed instead, and often scours deeper along the rock.

Meanders keep their proportions. On creeks and on the Mississippi alike, the distance from one bend to the next bend on the same side is roughly ten to fourteen times the channel's width. You can check it on a satellite map: measure the width of a river on a straight stretch, then the distance from one bend to the next bend on the same side, and divide. A river 50 metres wide should repeat its bends about every 600 metres.[^sinuosity]

Why a straight river starts to bend at all is a harder question than why a bend grows. Any small kink would grow by the feedback above, and in laboratory channels of sand a straight stream soon builds bars that alternate from side to side and steer the flow into a wiggle. But a lasting single winding channel proved hard to make in a laboratory: for decades the experimental rivers braided instead, until experimenters in the 2000s grew alfalfa sprouts on their banks.[^alfalfa] What starts a river's first bends, and how much its banks must resist for them to last, are still argued over.

Below the glaciers of Mount Rainier the White does not meander at all. It runs across a wide bed of grey gravel, split into many shallow channels that part and rejoin around bars and shift with every flood. The Carbon on Rainier's north side and the Hoh in the Olympics look the same. A river like this is **braided**.

A river braids when it is given more sand and gravel than one channel can carry, on a slope steep enough that even ordinary floods can move its bed. Glaciers grind rock to gravel and silt, and the steep slopes of a volcano slump into its rivers, so rivers fed from Rainier carry enormous loads. Lesson 4's grains and speeds are at work: when the flow slackens, the coarsest gravel drops in mid-channel and builds a bar, the water splits around it, and each thread builds bars of its own. Banks of loose gravel give way easily, so the river spreads wide and shallow. A meandering river is the other case: a gentler slope and a lighter load of mostly fine sediment, between banks held together by mud and roots.

In 1957 Luna Leopold and Gordon Wolman of the US Geological Survey compared the slopes and flows of many rivers and found a dividing line: for the same discharge, a braided river runs on a steeper slope than a meandering one, and the bigger the river, the gentler the slope at which braiding begins.[^leopold] Later work added the supply of sediment and the strength of the banks.

blocks.caption: A river seen from above, with its slope and its supply of sand and gravel. The dot on the chart below is the river drawn above it. A sketch of the rule, for a river with a flow of about 300 cubic metres a second at its banks' brim: the line is Leopold and Wolman's, and the effect of sediment supply is drawn roughly.
blocks.task: Make the river braid, then make it meander

blocks.text: One river can do both along its length. Downstream, as the slope eases and the coarse gravel drops out, braids give way to a single winding channel. The White still braids below the mountain; the lower Green, which used to carry it, meandered across the nearly flat floor of the Kent valley.

blocks.caption: Rivers of western Washington, by the shape of their channels.

options.ask: Braided, meandering, or held in place?

items.name: The White below Mount Rainier
items.why: Glacier-ground gravel and a steep slope: a wide grey bed of shifting threads.

items.name: The Snoqualmie between Fall City and Duvall
items.clue: a flat valley floor, muddy banks
items.why: A gentle slope across a broad, flat valley floor, with old loops and sloughs on both sides.

items.name: The Hoh in the Olympic rain forest
items.clue: glaciers on Mount Olympus, lots of gravel
items.why: Glacial gravel and huge logs keep it splitting and rejoining across a wide valley floor.

items.name: The lower Skagit near Mount Vernon
items.clue: farms right up to its banks
items.why: Dikes and riprap fix it in place to protect the farms of the delta; it would wander otherwise.

items.name: The Carbon on Rainier's north side
items.why: Like the White, a steep river overloaded with gravel from the mountain.

items.name: The Sauk below Darrington
items.clue: wide forested valley, loops and side channels
items.why: A gentler valley floor where single channels swing in loops and leave old channels behind.

blocks.text: Before settlers cleared them, the rivers of the Puget lowland were full of wood. Trees hundreds of years old toppled in as banks were undercut, and big logs lodged on bars and caught others until jams of hundreds of trees spanned a channel. In the 1870s settlers spent years cutting apart the great jams that blocked the lower Skagit near Mount Vernon, to open the river to steamboats.[^skagit] A jam does to a river what a boulder does to a creek: it turns the water aside, scours a pool beneath it and drops gravel above it. Much of the pattern of pools, bars and side channels in a wild river here is made by wood.

A jam can do something bigger. A river with a heavy load drops a little gravel on its own bed in each flood, and when it spills over its banks it drops sand right beside the channel, where the overflowing water first slows. Over decades the channel can come to sit on a low ridge of its own making, higher than the floodplain on either side. Water poured over the side would run away from the river, downhill. If a jam blocks the channel during a flood, the water goes over the side, down to the low ground, and if that new path is shorter or steeper it can capture the whole river. A river jumping to a new course is an **avulsion**.

blocks.caption: An avulsion, cut across a valley floor. A river that builds its bed up above the land beside it can be tipped out of its channel by a jam during a flood, and takes the lower ground. Heights exaggerated.

blocks.text: That is what happened at Auburn. The White came out of the foothills onto a broad, almost level floor of its own gravel and of mudflows from Mount Rainier,[^osceola] with two downhill routes open to it, north to Seattle and south to Tacoma. The Stuck was probably an older course of the White itself. The jam of 1906 did not push the river uphill. It blocked one of two nearly equal downhill paths during a flood, and the river took the other.

Most lowland rivers around the Sound are now held in place. The lower Skagit runs between dikes, and the Green through Kent and the Puyallup through Sumner and Fife between levees. A levee stops a river wandering and keeps its floods off the land behind it, until a bigger flood overtops or breaks it; the Columbia branch comes back to that. Engineers now also build log jams on purpose, to deepen pools and to steer rivers away from roads and banks.

blocks.caption: Six questions on how rivers move
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: Why do tea leaves gather in the middle of the bottom of a stirred cup?
choices: Near the bottom, friction slows the swirl, so the inward push from the higher water at the rim wins and the bottom water flows inward, carrying the leaves
The spinning water throws the leaves outward first, and they bounce off the wall of the cup back toward the middle
The leaves are heavier than water, and the bottom of a cup is lowest in the middle, so they slide down into the dip
items.why: The swirling water makes the surface a dish, higher at the rim. That pushes inward at every depth. Up high the fast swirl's outward push wins; at the bottom, where friction slows the water, the inward push wins and the water creeps to the middle.

items.ask: On a bend of a meandering river, where is the water deepest, and why?
choices: Against the outside bank, where the surface water plunges down and scours a pool
Along the inside bank, where the river slows and the water piles up
In the middle of the channel, equally far from both banks
items.why: The secondary flow drives surface water toward the outside bank and down it, digging a pool and a steep cut bank. The bed flow carries sediment to the inside, building a shallow point bar.

items.ask: Which explanation best accounts for meander bends growing larger over time?
choices: A sharper bend drives stronger secondary flow, which erodes the outside bank faster and sharpens the bend further
Floods carry gravel that pushes the inside bank outward, so each bend is pushed wider from inside
Water seeping into the banks softens them evenly, and the bend sags outward under its own weight
items.why: It is a feedback. The channel moves toward the outside of its bend, the bend sharpens, and a sharper bend erodes its outside bank faster still, until a cutoff ends the loop.

items.ask: How does an oxbow lake form?
choices: A loop grows until only a narrow neck of land is left; a flood cuts across the neck and the old loop is cut off
A landslide dams a meander and the water behind it backs up into a curved lake
Wind blows sand across the inside of a bend until the bend is closed off from the river
items.why: This is a neck cutoff. The river takes the short cut across the neck, and the abandoned loop, plugged with sediment at both ends, is left as a curved lake.

items.ask: The White below Mount Rainier is braided, while the Snoqualmie near Duvall meanders. Which difference best explains this?
choices: The White is steeper and carries far more gravel than one channel can move, so it drops bars and splits around them
The White carries less water, so it cannot fill one channel and spreads out thinly instead
The Snoqualmie flows north, and rivers flowing north are turned into bends by the Earth's rotation
items.why: Braiding comes with a steep slope and a heavy load of coarse sediment, from Rainier's glaciers and slopes. The Snoqualmie crosses a flat valley with a lighter, finer load and muddy, rooted banks.

items.ask: In November 1906 a log jam near Auburn sent the White River south to the Puyallup instead of north to the Duwamish. What made this possible?
choices: The valley floor there was nearly level, with two downhill routes, and the jam blocked one of them during a flood
The jam raised the water so high that it flowed uphill over a ridge into the Puyallup valley
The flood dug a new tunnel through the gravel under the valley floor to the Puyallup
items.why: A jam cannot push water uphill. At Auburn the White ran on a broad, almost flat floor between two routes, and the jam tipped it from one downhill path to the other: an avulsion.

baer.title: Einstein and Baer's law
baer.text: Einstein's paper of 1926 was titled, in German, "The cause of the formation of meanders in the courses of rivers and of the so-called Baer's law". Karl Ernst von Baer had argued in the 1860s that rivers in the northern hemisphere wear away their right banks faster because of the Earth's rotation. Einstein agreed that the rotation adds a small push of the same kind as a bend's, but the bend's own secondary flow is far stronger.

thomson.title: James Thomson
thomson.text: James Thomson (1822 to 1892) was a professor of engineering in Belfast and later Glasgow, and a designer of water turbines. His 1876 paper to the Royal Society, on the windings of rivers in plains, described the flow toward the outside bank at the surface and toward the inside along the bed; he went on to show it in model channels.

lidar.title: Lidar
lidar.text: Lidar measures the ground by timing laser pulses fired from an aircraft. Some pulses slip between the leaves to the ground, so the trees can be stripped away and the bare floodplain shown as a shaded relief. Washington's Department of Natural Resources publishes these maps on its lidar portal, where old channels and scroll bars stand out clearly.

sinuosity.title: Sinuosity
sinuosity.text: A river's **sinuosity** is the length of its channel divided by the straight length of its valley. A straight channel scores 1; geomorphologists usually call a river meandering above about 1.5, and a loop just before its neck is cut off can push a reach above 3. The bends' radius is typically two to three channel widths.

alfalfa.title: Rivers in a sandbox
alfalfa.text: Experimental river channels in sand and gravel tend to braid, because nothing holds their banks. In the 2000s, groups at the University of Minnesota and the University of California at Berkeley got a single channel to keep meandering in the laboratory by sprouting alfalfa on its floodplain, and by adding fine sediment that filled in the low ground. The roots and the mud did what forests and silt do on a real floodplain.

leopold.title: Leopold and Wolman's line
leopold.text: In metric units their line is close to slope = 0.012 × Q^-0.44, with Q the discharge in cubic metres a second at which the river just fills its banks (lesson 2's discharge). For a river carrying 300 cubic metres a second that is a slope of about 0.1 percent, a metre of drop in a kilometre; steeper than that, it tends to braid.

skagit.title: The Skagit jams
skagit.text: Accounts from the time describe two great jams below Mount Vernon, so old that trees grew on top of them, which settlers cut apart in the 1870s. Opening them let steamboats reach the upper valley. Similar jams on most Puget lowland rivers were cleared in the same decades, and the rivers ran faster and simpler afterward.

osceola.title: Mudflows from Rainier
osceola.text: About 5,600 years ago the Osceola Mudflow poured off Mount Rainier when part of the summit collapsed, and spread across the lowland as far as Auburn and Kent, burying the valley under metres of mud and rock. The White and the Puyallup have been working across that surface ever since. The Geology course covers lahars like it.
